title: Russia's diesel export ban: the middle-distillate chain behind a crude-priced headline
thesis: Russia, normally a 900,000 to 1,000,000 barrel-a-day exporter of diesel and gasoil, has banned those exports and kept rolling the ban forward as Ukrainian drones hold refineries offline; June exports had already fallen to about 580,000 bpd and the ban puts up to 36% of Russia's total oil-product export volumes at risk. The market read this as an oil story and priced crude, but the shortage is in the PRODUCT, and the product is the fuel of freight, agriculture and mining. The consequence is already realized rather than forecast: the US diesel crack spread settled at a record $102.20 per barrel against a normal $20 to $40 range, and European diesel margins passed $60 per barrel. The unmapped part is who structurally fills a middle-distillate gap: complex refiners with the hydrocracking and desulfurization capacity to make ultra-low-sulfur diesel, the Long Range product tankers absorbing the ton-mile inflation as short-haul Baltic cargoes are replaced by Persian Gulf and India long hauls, and the catalyst, turnaround and refinery-services suppliers who benefit when every remaining unit is run to maximum.
why_now: The ban stopped being an episode and became a pattern: it was extended again on 2026-08-29, to 2026-09-30 for producers, with non-producer diesel and motor gasoline already banned to 2027-01-31 and jet fuel to end-November 2026. The physical damage is what makes it roll: Russian refineries processed an average of 3.91 million barrels of crude per day in early July, more than 1.4 million bpd below the previous year's average, and several remain offline after repeated drone attacks. Meanwhile the replacement trade has visibly repriced: the Platts LR2 index rose from $57,204 per day at the beginning of June to $97,872 per day on July 14, and US diesel inventories entering late August 2026 sat at their lowest level since 1996.
retail_gap: Coverage of Russian energy disruption is saturated at the CRUDE layer: the oil price, sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil, the shadow fleet, the price cap. The refined-PRODUCT layer beneath it is covered in energy trade press (OilPrice, S&P Global, Platts assessments, tanker-market blogs) and in refiner earnings calls, and rarely reaches general financial media as an investable chain. The specific structural scarcity, ultra-low-sulfur-diesel-capable hydrocracking capacity that takes years to build, is discussed as a technical fact in industry commentary and almost never as the reason a margin is durable. Retail exposure to the theme, where it exists at all, is to the crude complex rather than to conversion capacity or to product shipping.

unmappedness.rationale: The occurrence could not be less obscure: a government decree reported by every wire the day it was signed, inside the most covered geopolitical story of the decade. Selection is on the chain, not the event. The crude chain behind Russian sanctions is exhaustively mapped; the middle-distillate chain is not. Three separable links share this one headline and are routinely collapsed into it: conversion capacity (which refiners actually have the hydrocracking and desulfurization units to lengthen the barrel into diesel, as against those merely enjoying a cyclical crack), the Long Range product-tanker owners capturing the route lengthening, and the catalyst, turnaround and refinery-services layer that a run-maximisation regime pulls forward. Held at 76 rather than higher because the headline refiner names have already had one quarter of very visible results, so the first link is only partly dark; the tanker and services links are darker.

evidence.claim: The diesel crack spread record high of $102.20 per barrel on August 17, 2026 marked the first occasion in history that refining margins for distillate fuel exceeded triple digits, against a previous all-time record of approximately $89 per barrel set in October 2022 and a normal range of roughly $20 to $40 per barrel; U.S. diesel inventories entering late August 2026 stood at their lowest level since 1996.
evidence.source_name: Discovery Alert, Diesel Crack Spread Shatters Records With $102 High in 2026
source_excerpt: The diesel crack spread record high of $102.20 per barrel on August 17, 2026 marked the first occasion in history that refining margins for distillate fuel exceeded triple digits.
The previous all-time record of approximately $89 per barrel, set in October 2022, has been surpassed by roughly 15%.
Under stable market conditions, diesel crack spreads typically trade in a range of roughly $20 to $40 per barrel.
U.S. diesel inventories entering late August 2026 stood at their lowest level since 1996, a 30-year trough that dramatically amplified the market's price response.

evidence.claim: The shift in diesel supply sourcing from Baltic-to-Europe short-haul trips on Medium Range tankers to Persian Gulf or India-to-Europe long-haul voyages on Long Range tankers has absorbed significant LR capacity and significantly boosts ton-mile demand, with LR2s commanding high premiums; the Platts LR2 index for vessels without scrubbers and not eco-designed rose from $57,204 per day at the beginning of June to $97,872 per day on July 14.
evidence.source_name: IndexBox, Russia Fuel Export Ban and Ukraine Attacks Reshape Clean Tanker Markets in 2026
source_excerpt: The broader consequences for mainstream tanker markets are that the shift in diesel supply sourcing from Baltic-to-Europe short-haul trips on Medium Range tankers to Persian Gulf or India-to-Europe long-haul voyages on Long Range tankers has absorbed significant LR capacity
LR2s, specifically, are commanding high premiums because of their better economics on long-distance journeys.
The Platts LR2 index, for vessels without scrubbers and not eco-designed, rose from $57,204 per day at the beginning of June to $97,872 per day on July 14.
These extended journeys significantly boost ton-mile demand for conventional tankers.

TASTE-002 (no Taiwan chip-concentration diversification thesis): does not bind on subject, and its underlying PRINCIPLE is the one worth checking here, because it is the rule that refuses a standing macro story with no dated discrete event. This card passes that test on its own terms: the occurrence is a dated decree extended on 2026-08-29 with stated expiries (2026-09-30, 2027-01-31, end-November 2026), not the ambient 'Russia sanctions' narrative. Nothing was overridden and no rule conflicts with this card.

Dedupe against SIG-20260829-04 (Hormuz closure), the only other energy-disruption card on disk. Separable and kept separate: SIG-20260829-04 is CRUDE rerouting, marine war-risk underwriting and piracy, with a different actor and a different trigger. This is a REFINED-PRODUCT export ban whose chain is conversion capacity and clean product tankers. Both cards share the fact that tanker ton-miles lengthen, which is the one place a chain build must state the interaction explicitly rather than double-count it: dirty and clean tanker fleets are different vessels and different owners, and a map that merges them will invent an issuer census that does not exist.

Honest weakness on the clock, stated so a chain build inherits it rather than discovers it. Every DATED commitment in this occurrence is short: the producer ban runs to 2026-09-30, the non-producer and gasoline ban to 2027-01-31, jet fuel to end-November 2026. The 2 to 4 year horizon on this card rests on the PHYSICAL side, not the administrative one: refinery capacity destroyed by repeated drone strikes and conversion capacity that takes years to build. The main invalidation is named in the sources rather than invented: shadow-fleet tankers displaced from the old short-haul Russian trade are reported as waiting for Russian loadings to recover rather than exiting, which is latent capacity that can re-enter and compress rates when the ban eases.
